messages.subject: Re: Getting t-test output
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the quick reply.
I skimmed the paper, and I agree with everything about t-tests;  
central tendency gives an incomplete picture.  t-tests are necessary  
but not sufficient, as you say in your paper, and I used them as a  
first glance at balance --- it's handy to have a single number for  
each variable to decide how much revision is necessary.

This data's unfortunately confidential, but I'll look into  
replicating the error in some other data or adding some high variance  
noise or something.

Janet

On Sep 30, 2007, at 7:56 PM, Kosuke Imai wrote:

>> 1.  It looks like the package is now entirely non-parametric, but  
>> is there any way to get the old output for MatchIt including sd  
>> and t-test results, as shown here?
>>
>> http://gking.harvard.edu/matchit/docs/Propensity_Score_Match.html
>
> This is an old site. Please look at the new site: http:// 
> gking.harvard.edu/matchit/  As for t-tests, in a paper that is  
> forthcoming at Journal of the Royal Statistical Society (Series A),  
> we argue that t-tests should not be used when examining balance.  
> See http://imai.princeton.edu/research/balance.html for details.
>
>> The empirical QQ plots do seem more helpful than tests of central  
>> tendency, but I find it hard to evaluate a few dozen covariates  
>> visually.  Are there any guidelines for interpreting the eQQ  
>> summary statistics?
>
> eQQ is basically the differences in quantiles between the treatment  
> and control group covariate distributions. They are all on the  
> scale on which each variable is measured. That is, there is no  
> transformation or standardization, and so you can interpret them as  
> they are.

after running -matchit-, I'm writing out the match matrix.
write.dta(data.frame(m.out$match.matrix),"mmatrix.dta")

I want to use the file to create a matched file in Stata--I want to 
analyze treatment v. matched comparison on a pair-by-pair basis. (I'm 
doing some of the sensitivity analyses in Rosenbaum's book.)

stata, I get

41. 818

Maybe there's still some new math at Harvard, and I didn't get the memo.

any suggestions? /m

messages.subject: Re: befuddled by match.matrix
messages.body_plain:
Your original data frame has unique row names corresponding to each of
the observations, which are used in match.matrix.  Depending on the
format of your input data these may or may not be numbers.  The row
names of match.matrix correspond to the names of the treated, and each
of the cells corresponds to a name of matched controls.

So for example:

> data(lalonde)
> row.names(lalonde)

  [1] "NSW1"    "NSW2"   . . .  "NSW185"   "PSID1"   "PSID2"  . . . "PSID429"

> foo <- matchit(treat ~ re74 + re75 + educ, data=lalonde)
> data.frame(foo$match.matrix)
            X1
NSW1   PSID352
NSW2   PSID271
NSW3   PSID418
NSW4   PSID382
NSW5   PSID355
...

Dan

messages.body_plain:
thanks, dan--

FYI for the rest of the list:

    pscore<-read.dta("working.dta")        

    m.out<- matchit(Y~<xvar> , model="optimal" , data=pscore)
    m.data<-match.data(m.out)
    summary(m.out)

    mm<-m.out$match.matrix
    tx<-as.numeric(row.names(mm))
    m<-cbind(tx,as.numeric(mm))
    m[1:5,]

    write.dta(data.frame(m),"mmatrix.dta")

That gave me what I wanted: a file with one record per match that 
recorded the id's for the tx and comparison cases.

You might be interested in knowing that when I did Rosenbaum sensitivity 
analyses (like in his book), the full matching pairs were *much* less 
sensitive to unobserved heterogeneity than some of the greedy matching 
alternatives I had used in Stata.

Very cool (at least to this nerd!)
regards,
michael

messages.subject: Re: which variables, and how many, to match on?
messages.subject_clean: which variables, and how many, to match on?
messages.body_plain:
In theory, there is no limit as to the number of variables you can include 
as the variables you match on. In fact, a typical recommendation is that 
you include as many relevant control variables as possible so that the 
assumption of ignorability (no omitted variables) is likely to hold.  In a 
small sample, however, you will not be able to match on all of your 
variables very well when you have many control variables to match on. In 
such situations, it is helpful to use substantive knowledge and identify a 
small number of variables that are known to strongly affect both the 
treatment and the outcome variables.  Then, you can exactly match on these 
variables while using the propensity score to balance the others.  This 
can be done for example using the exact restriction option in matchit()

Hope this helps,

messages.subject: Re: which variables, and how many, to match on?
messages.subject_clean: which variables, and how many, to match on?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Casey,
Here are my thoughts on this issue.  It is a matter of some debate in the
matching literature, though, so others may have other ideas.

1.  Match on as many variables as you, and certainly check the balance on
all of the ones you have observed, even if you don't actually match on them.
This can be done in MatchIt using the "addlvariables" option in the
summary() command.

2.  If you have enough observations, you should be able to match on all 40
variables.  

3.  People generally stay away from selecting the variables to include based
on analyses of the outcome data in their dataset, to avoid modeling the
outcome (or even analyzing the outcome) before finishing the matching.
Instead, the selection is usually based on which variables are a priori
believed to affect both treatment assignment and the outcome (true
confounders).  Some research has shown that it is better to be inclusive in
the matching, in that it is better to include irrelevant variables than it
is to exclude relevant ones, but again, this is a topic of recent research
and some recent simulations have shown that including variables that are
independent of the outcome can be inefficient.

4.  In situations I have been in where we had more variables than we really
could match on, I have made a priority list of the variables on which it was
particularly important to get good balance (e.g., pre-treatment measures of
the outcome variables of interest or other variables I believe are highly
predictive of the outcome).  Then fit a propensity score model with those
important ones, and check the balance on all of the variables.  If there are
some other variables that are badly balanced in the resulting matched data,
include them in a second iteration of the propensity score. Iterate until
you get good balance overall.

I hope this helps,
Liz

messages.body_plain:
I'd add that, unlike controlling for variables in linear regression or 
other parametric techniques, including variables that are more highly 
collinear with each other in matching will not explode your standard 
errors and make your analysis less efficient.  So some of the 40 vars you 
have might all be pretty closely related, in which case its like 
controlling for just one or a few.

Also, if you intend to run a parametric analysis after matching, as we 
recommend, and you have a list of variables you intend to include in that 
analysis, you should probably match on all those variables prior to the 
parametric analysis.  If you don't, then you're controlling via the 
assumptions of your model.  if there aren't enough observations after 
matching on all those variables, then you may be stuck with the 
controlling via the model.

Gary
